content:
After shooting a series of portrait photos to test the larger aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro, I had originally planned to wait until dark to see if letting in more light would shorten the capture time for Night mode shots.

I later postponed that test because something far more interesting happened: the extremely rare sight of a cruise ship passing under Tower Bridge in London. That presented the perfect opportunity to test the new model's Night video capabilities...

Over the years, the iPhone has evolved into an extraordinarily powerful camera, but there has always been a significant gap between the image quality achievable during the day and at night, whether shooting stills or video.

Apple has put a great deal of effort into low-light still photography over the years, and the results really show. Given the extremely small sensor, the iPhone's current low-light shooting ability is already remarkably good. The addition of Night mode portraits in 2020 also deserves credit.

Generally speaking, computational photography is the secret behind many of the iPhone's low-light capabilities. Although we think we're just taking a single shot, the phone is actually capturing an entire series of frames and then combining the different exposures into a single image.

However, the challenge with video is far greater. When we're shooting at least 24 frames per second, and usually capturing moving footage, it's very difficult for the phone to capture multiple exposures for the same frame and then composite them together. That is why Night video quality inevitably lags so far behind still photography.

That said, Apple continues to invest significant resources in improving this area, and each generation delivers better Night video performance. The iPhone 18 Pro not only benefits from Apple's annual improvements to video processing, but also features a larger aperture to let in more light. Although the gain is less than one full stop, every additional photon counts when it comes to video.

The full clip played at normal speed runs for more than nine minutes, and I didn't want to rely on the device's excellent video stabilisation for that long, so I secured a small tripod firmly to the top of the railing. I have sped the footage up to 10 times normal speed, bringing the length down to 96 seconds, but kept a few sections at original speed so you can appreciate the extremely precise manoeuvring being carried out by the tugboats.

How did it turn out? Not perfect, but undoubtedly another step forward in the evolution of image quality. Of course, people like me will keep zooming in and complaining that certain details look rather mushy close up, but that kind of talk is really insignificant. Ordinary viewers watching this kind of footage would simply enjoy the spectacular scene in front of them without a single complaint about picture quality. When I review low-light video from a few generations ago, the difference is nothing short of night and day.

So, Night video performance still hasn't reached the ideal level I have in mind, but every generation keeps getting better, and this one is no exception. In fact, even in such a challenging environment, we have easily crossed the threshold of 'good enough for most people to enjoy'.
